corpus.source: PyPI source distributions (sdist) of the top packages by download count. Wheels are never used as a fallback: a wheel is build output, so for anything with a build step it is not the tree the author wrote. Packages publishing no sdist are skipped by the fetch driver, as Java skips artifacts with no sources jar.
corpus.ranking: hugovk/top-pypi-packages (top-pypi-packages.min.json), the standard published extract of the public PyPI download dataset
corpus.ranking_note: PyPI's own API exposes no download counts; the numbers live in the public BigQuery/ClickHouse dataset. This is therefore the same KIND of metric as crates.io and npm downloads — traffic — unlike Java's dependent-repos proxy. The dataset's own last_update is printed by `treebank rank` and belongs in any sweep write-up.
corpus.files_note: .py only, the single extension tree-sitter-python's tree-sitter.json claims. .pyi stubs are also Python and this same grammar parses them; they are excluded for now so classify() matches what the grammar advertises, and adding them would be a deliberate change with its own sweep evidence. Paths containing a _vendor/ or _vendored/ component are excluded for the reason javascript excludes bundles: pip and others vendor whole dependency sets, so a failure there is attributed to the wrong package and the same code is already in the corpus under its real owner.
corpus.oracle: tools/py-oracle/check.py — CPython's own front end via compile(src, path, 'exec'), the exact call Python makes to turn a module's text into code. TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. It never imports, executes or resolves a name, so a missing dependency is not an error and each file is judged entirely on its own text.
corpus.oracle_version_note: The interpreter version IS the language version and is load-bearing exactly as generate_cli is: `match` is 3.10+, the walrus 3.8+, parenthesised context managers 3.10 in practice. A file needing syntax newer than this interpreter is recorded as corpus noise, which is the honest answer. Bumping it is treated like a patch: full sweep, before/after numbers, ledger entry.
corpus.packages_note: 500 requested; 492 resolved. The rest publish no sdist, which the fetch driver skips rather than falling back to a wheel.
corpus.remaining_gaps_note: 5 gap files remain, in two families, both in the external scanner / lexer rather than in grammar.js, and both left deliberately. (a) An f-string format specifier that begins with '=' — f"{num:=.2Uf}", f"{v:=>10}" — because ':=' is lexed as the walrus operator before format_specifier's ':' is considered (1 file). (b) Backslash line continuations interacting with indentation, e.g. `else:\` followed by an indented body, and an attribute access split as `tester.x. \` across lines (4 files, all parser/formatter test fixtures from ruff and executing). Neither reproduces in a small isolated snippet — both need the surrounding indentation state — and both sit in scanner.c, where the blast radius is every Python file. They are the next fix agent's queue, with repros recorded in LOCAL-PATCHES.md.
corpus.oracle_note: Deliberately compile() and not ast.parse(). CPython enforces a set of rules AFTER the parser that are still SyntaxErrors and still make a file unusable as a module: `return`/`await` outside a function, `_ = *[42]` ("can't use starred expression here"), a bare `except:` that is not last, duplicate parameter names. ast.parse accepts all of them. Measured: 11 of the 30 files the first sweep called grammar gaps were files CPython would refuse to run — fragments and deliberately-invalid fixtures shipped as test data by ruff, black, pylint and parso. The cost, stated plainly: a file that is compile-invalid for one reason AND has a real grammar gap for another is now noise rather than a gap, so gap_files can under-report. Same direction as C's indeterminate collapse, and the safe one — the sweep can miss a grammar bug, it can never invent one.
corpus.oracle_cost: 1.23 s per 1000 files (ast.parse was 0.97 s); still firmly Tier A

grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.summary: tree-sitter-python deliberately parses Python 2 as well as Python 3; the oracle (CPython 3.12) rejects Python 2. So for this language the grammar accepts a strict superset of what the oracle calls valid — the reverse of the usual relationship, and it needs stating because it changes what the negative corpus can contain.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.evidence: grammar.js carries print_statement (line 204) and exec_statement (line 443) rules, and upstream ships examples/python2-grammar.py and examples/mixed-spaces-tabs.py as fixtures. Measured: the grammar accepts `print "hello"`, `exec "x = 1"`, `except IOError, e:`, a tab/space indent mix, `class A:` with an unindented body, and an inconsistent dedent — all six of which CPython 3.12 rejects.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.why_this_is_safe: A sweep gap is 'grammar rejected it AND the oracle accepted it'. This asymmetry runs the other way — grammar accepts, oracle rejects — so it can never manufacture a gap, and gap_files stays exact. It is not the accepts-invalid-code drift GRAMMARS.md warns about, because it is upstream's deliberate design rather than an optimization artifact.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.cost: The negative corpus cannot contain Python 2 constructs or indentation errors, because the grammar will not reject them and by upstream's design should not. test/negative/ is therefore restricted to syntax that is invalid in BOTH Python 2 and 3 — 12 files, each verified rejected by the oracle and by the grammar.

patches.title: comment at column zero inside a block
patches.origin: treebank; found by the first top-500 PyPI sweep

evidence.diagnosis: The external scanner only treats a '#' as a comment when INDENT, DEDENT, NEWLINE or EXCEPT is a valid symbol. After a decorator the parser expects only another decorator or a def/class, so none of those is valid, the comment line is not consumed as a comment, and its column-0 indentation is taken as the line's indentation - which dedents out of the class body and puts the decorator in an ERROR. CPython's tokenizer ignores comment-only lines entirely for indentation, at any column, so this is valid Python that the grammar rejected. The fix adds found_end_of_line to that condition: once an end of line has been seen, a '#' always starts a comment line. Behaviour before an end of line - the trailing `foo = bar # comment` case the condition was written for - is unchanged.
evidence.evidence_note: One file in 70,423, and zero regressions: the before/after sweeps were run over the identical corpus with only this patch removed and restored. A small number, stated as measured rather than dressed up - the value is that it is a real correctness fix with a five-line repro, two lines of scanner change, a corpus test, and no cost anywhere else.
evidence.upstream_status: not yet reported upstream; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha

patches.title: slices in a generic type application
patches.origin: treebank; found by the top-500 PyPI sweep

evidence.repro:
a: int32_t[:] = f()
foo: Bar[:, :, :]
def to_chars(s) -> char_type[:]: ...
def compute(x: my_type[:, ::1]): ...
evidence.diagnosis: generic_type took $.type_parameter, whose elements are $.type, and $.type has no slice. Since generic_type carries prec(1) it also shadowed the plain subscript reading, so `int[:]` had no path at all. A slice inside a subscript is ordinary valid Python — Subscript(Name, Slice()) — and Cython's pure-Python mode uses it heavily for memoryviews. Fixed by giving generic_type its own argument list that admits $.slice, aliased back to the type_parameter node name so the tree shape consumers query is unchanged. The PEP 695 declaration sites (def f[T], class C[T]) keep the strict $.type_parameter, verified by `def f[:](): ...` still being rejected.

patches.title: PEP 646 unpacking beyond a bare name
patches.origin: treebank; found by the top-500 PyPI sweep

evidence.repro:
def foo(*args: *(int or str)): ...
data[*(x := y)]
u = tuple[*Ts]
evidence.diagnosis: Two halves of the same feature. splat_type accepted only a bare $.identifier, so `*(int or str)` and `*tuple[int, ...]` failed; it now also takes a parenthesized_expression or a generic_type. Listing alternatives rather than widening to $.type is deliberate — widening wrapped the identifier case in a `type` node and broke two upstream corpus tests, which is a tree-shape change consumers' queries would feel. Separately, subscript admitted only expression or slice, so `data[*x]` had no path; it now also takes $.list_splat. `data[*]` and `def f(*args: *): ...` are still rejected.

patches.title: starred expressions in bare tuples and targets
patches.origin: treebank; found by the top-500 PyPI sweep

evidence.diagnosis: $.list_splat is not an $.expression, so an element of a bare tuple could never be a starred expression. `a = *b,` appeared to work only because a bare name is also a valid assignment-target pattern and the parser took the pattern branch; `a = *[1],` had no path at all. expression_list now takes choice($.expression, $.list_splat), matching CPython's star_expressions. Separately list_splat_pattern accepted only identifier/subscript/attribute, so the legal target `*[], b = (1,)` failed; it now also takes list_pattern and tuple_pattern, matching CPython's target_with_star_atom.
